title: Brahma's promise
word: the crow and the first verse
hookLine: Brahma tells the troubled poet the verse was meant; why Hindus still recite the Ramayana aloud
carry: reciting the Ramayana is itself an act of worship
tomorrow: why does a king with everything turn to the sacred fire?

cards: Valmiki goes back to his hermitage, but he can't let it go. He bathes, he sits, and the verse keeps playing in his head, and he is uneasy about the curse he spoke.
You know the feeling: a sentence you said today, replaying at night. Then a visitor arrives. Brahma himself, the creator, four-faced, the one the whole world comes from.
And Valmiki, still lost in the bird's grief, can't stop saying the verse, even in front of him.

teach.h: THE VERSE CAME FROM ME, SAYS BRAHMA.
teach.b: Brahma smiles and settles it. Don't be troubled, he says. That verse came from me; it was meant to.
Now tell the whole story of Rama, as Narada told it to you, in this same meter. Not one word you speak in this poem will be false.

teach.h: AS LONG AS MOUNTAINS AND RIVERS.
teach.b: Then the promise people still quote: as long as mountains stand and rivers flow on the earth, so long will the story of Rama be told. Valmiki sits on a seat of sacred grass and turns inward.
The whole story comes to him in vision. The tradition gives the count: twenty-four thousand verses. Two boys live in his hermitage, twins with beautiful voices, Kusha and Lava.

teach.h: TWO BOYS SING IT BY HEART.
teach.b: He teaches them the whole poem by heart, and they sing it to sages and later in a king's court. Here's the turn: the twins are Rama's own sons, though Rama doesn't know them yet. The story will be sung to its own hero.
And that's why, for Hindus, the Ramayana isn't only a book to read.
It's a story to say aloud and to hear, and doing that is worship. Families and temples hold readings. Many recite one book, often the Sundara Kanda, Hanuman's book, as a prayer.
And before a reading, an old verse honors Valmiki as a cuckoo, sitting on the branch of poetry, singing Rama, Rama, sweetly.
So if you have seen a grandmother read the Ramayana aloud, verse by verse, even the long lists, that is not slowness.
It is prayer, and sitting beside her and listening counts too.

how: Many Hindus recite or listen to the Ramayana at home and in temples as an act of devotion, sometimes one book such as the Sundara Kanda, sometimes the whole across several days; readings often open with a verse honoring Valmiki, and the tradition of reciters traces itself back to Kusha and Lava.

games.why: Brahma promised the story would be told as long as mountains stand, and the first to tell it sang it by heart. saying it aloud is devotion.

practice: Sit like Valmiki on his grass seat. If you pray, say Rama, Rama softly, the way the cuckoo in that old verse sings it, or say a line of a prayer you know by heart, and hear it as you say it.
If you don't pray, just listen: play a minute of someone chanting the Ramayana or the Sundara Kanda, and hear it the way the sages heard the twins.

wordCard.voice: Today's word: the crow and the first verse. The bird in the story is really a krauncha, a water bird, not a crow. Brahma tells Valmiki the verse was meant, and gives him the whole story of Rama to tell in that same meter.

orig.note: Sanskrit śloka: verse, the epic meter of four quarters, eight syllables each.
